name: Malawi

most.note: Recommended for most people going to Malawi who haven't had it before. It spreads through food and water, and a good hotel doesn't remove the risk.
Check when you last had a tetanus, diphtheria and polio booster. If it was more than ten years ago and you'll be anywhere medical care is limited, a booster is recommended.
Spread through food and water. Recommended for most trips to Malawi, and especially if you're staying with family or eating away from the tourist trail.

some.note: Only for a few people: aid and health workers, and anyone going to an outbreak area with limited access to clean water.
Spread by daytime-biting mosquitoes, and bite avoidance is the main protection. Ask about the vaccine if you've had dengue before.
Worth considering for longer stays, for anyone who might need medical or dental treatment there, and for work with blood or needles.
Make sure you've had two doses of MMR. Measles is common in Malawi, and a UK adult who missed a dose can catch it.
Proof of polio vaccination can be asked for on arrival or departure. Check your booster is within ten years.
Worth considering if you'll be around animals, in rural areas or far from medical care, and for children, who are bitten more often. The course takes three or four weeks, so book early.
Only for a few people: under-16s staying three months or more with local people, and healthcare workers.

certificates: A yellow fever certificate is asked for from travellers aged 1 year and over arriving from a country with yellow fever risk, or after more than 12 hours in transit through one. Flying straight from the UK, you won't need one.

malaria.line: Malaria is present in parts of Malawi, and tablets are advised for some areas. Which areas, and whether you need them, is settled at your consultation.
